platform_note: 6 performance cores with Hyper-Threading plus 4 efficiency cores; Windows 11 chooses core placement (no affinity pinning); Lenovo Legion Balance power mode on AC power
checks_note: Sanitizers cannot run in the Windows MinGW-w64 toolchain, so the four C++ test programs were also compiled directly with g++ 13.3 under WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04 on the same laptop (outside CMake, -O1 -g). ASan+UBSan: all four passed with no report. TSan initially aborted with 'unexpected memory mapping' before running any test, a known incompatibility between GCC 13 TSan and newer kernel address layouts; it was rerun with address randomization disabled (setarch -R). TSan then passed all four programs (31 test cases, including the MCS enqueue-gap, barrier visibility and counter uniqueness tests) with zero data-race warnings. Logs are kept in validation-local/wsl-sanitizers.
lock_notes: With W=0 every prime call is inside the lock, so no speedup is possible: T(1) is about 87 ms and the best any lock can do is stay flat. TAS/TTAS stay within 87-108 ms up to P=14, while std::mutex jumps to about 119 ms as soon as P=2 and then stays flat, and MCS climbs to 169-178 ms at P=12-14.

With W=k outside calls, the critical section still holds 1/(k+1) of the work, so Amdahl's bound limits speedup to k+1. The spinlocks get close at low P: at W=1 they reach about 92 ms at P=2 (1.9x of the 2x bound), but std::mutex is slower than one thread (207-216 ms against 177 ms) for every P from 2 to 14. At W=4 (bound 5x) the best speedup is 3.9x (TTAS-backoff, P=6); at W=8 (bound 9x) it is 5.6x (TAS, P=12).

Past about 6-10 threads the time rises again for every lock. More waiters compete for the same cache line at each release, and this laptop has only 6 performance cores: higher P places threads on Hyper-Threading siblings and the slower efficiency cores. This placement explanation is a hypothesis consistent with the data, not a measured scheduler trace.

Saturation run (P=12/14/15/16, W=0, 5 measured runs each, 120 s timeout): TAS, TTAS, TTAS-backoff and std::mutex stay at 91-122 ms at every P, but MCS rises from 116 ms (P=12) to 333 ms (P=15) and 2,468 ms (P=16), with single P=16 runs between 0.18 s and 85 s. One warmup run of MCS at P=14 (per-thread, W=4) in the main study also hit the 60 s timeout. MCS hands the lock to one specific successor; when all 16 logical CPUs are busy spinning, that successor can be descheduled, and nobody can enter until Windows runs it again. This is the course's caveat that a preempted thread can block the MCS queue. TAS/TTAS instead let whichever running thread wins the flag enter.
sensitivity_notes: A short critical section (N=97) means very frequent handoffs. TAS degrades from 82 ms (P=1) to 244 ms (P=14) because every waiter keeps issuing test_and_set on the shared flag, while TTAS stays at 89-106 ms for P=2-14: reading before the RMW is what the slides predict should matter here. With a long critical section (N=10007) handoffs are rare and all locks stay within 87-115 ms except MCS at P=14 (225 ms).

In per-thread mode the total work grows with P, so times grow with P by design. std::mutex is the slowest lock at W=0 from P=2 to P=12, and MCS at P=14, W=4 jumps to 1,135 ms, the same oversubscription effect as above.

Exponential backoff gives TTAS a modest gain where retries are frequent: at N=97, W=4 it lowers the median from 160 to 144 ms at P=4 and from 246 to 226 ms at P=14. Elsewhere TTAS and TTAS-backoff are within run-to-run variation of each other.
barrier_notes: The custom barrier is much faster than std::barrier at every P>1: 5.5 million against 64 thousand episodes/s at P=2, and 435 thousand against 4.5 thousand at P=12. A centralized spinning barrier releases waiters with one cache-line update, while the libstdc++ std::barrier is designed to block waiting threads after a short spin, so each episode can pay an OS wake-up; its flat 4.5-6.6 thousand episodes/s from P=8 to P=16 is consistent with a wake-up-bound cost.

At P=1 the 54 million episodes/s only measure call overhead, since no other thread exists. At P=14 the custom barrier drops to 53 thousand episodes/s in the main run and 127 thousand in the saturation run, and to 22 thousand at P=16: one descheduled spinner delays the whole phase. The gap to std::barrier shrinks from about 100x to about 4x, which is the expected trade-off of busy waiting once threads exceed free CPUs.
counter_notes: No counter becomes faster with more threads: the fastest result overall is FAA with one thread (13.7 ms), because every increment updates one shared cache line and a single thread keeps it in its own cache.

CAS with backoff stays at 24-28 ms for all P, the lowest time from P=2 upward. After a failed CAS the losers pause, so the winner completes many increments in a row while it owns the cache line. This shows throughput, not fairness: backoff concentrates work in one thread at a time.

Plain CAS rises to 116 ms at P=14 because failed attempts waste cache-line transfers, while FAA stays at 33-45 ms since each increment is one RMW that cannot fail. The lock-based counters pay a lock and an unlock per increment: TAS-mutex reaches 731 ms at P=14, and MCS-mutex is already 304 ms at P=2 (37 ms at P=1) because every increment is a handoff to another core.
limitations: Limitations: one laptop with a hybrid CPU and no thread pinning, so the OS scheduler and core types add variation; background load was not controlled beyond closing heavy applications. Spin-wait results above 12 threads are dominated by scheduling, so P=15/16 is reported as a separate saturation study. Short runs remain sensitive to startup cost. There are no hardware performance counters, and finite tests and sanitizers do not prove every interleaving. The optional MPI-3 one-sided version was not implemented.
